It's a delicate balance. A lot of engineering goes into getting a reasonable answer out of a lattice calculation, and part of the reason is that the continuum limit is very far from obvious when you start from a regular grid. It's not just a matter of multiplying by the lattice spacing, because the continuum limit is only defined through the renormalisation group, and the form of the RG flow depends on the details of the regularisation. You can see this already in the fact that the critical exponents change when you alter the anisotropy of the lattice, even though the critical point itself (at a fixed coupling) doesn't move.
It's a little surprising how often people seem to miss this, because in most cases the effect is subtle. It's only when you look at correlation functions in very clean systems at criticality that the dependence on the lattice becomes hard to miss. The standard stories about why lattice QCD isn't yet in the continuum limit often focus on the chiral anomaly or the pion mass, but those are only two of the many indicators that we're still far from the continuum; the lattice artefacts show up in a lot of other ways too, some of which we understand and some of which we don't.

The Wilsonian picture says that we can purposefully integrate out the high-energy degrees of freedom, and that this will give us an effective low-energy theory which should describe the physics at lower energies. (I put "purposefully" there because, in the case of the universe, we didn't so much "purposefully" do this as it happened naturally as the universe expanded.) The standard example of this is the fact that the renormalisable theories are the ones where the UV divergences in a perturbative expansion can be absorbed into a finite number of counterterms. I still think this story is compelling because it can be told in a way that doesn't rely on the perturbative machinery that led to the discovery of the renormalisation group. You don't need to talk about Feynman diagrams or beta functions or the renormalisation group equation -- you can instead talk about the simple, intuitive idea that high-energy degrees of freedom should not affect low-energy observables, and that the details of how you regularise the UV are in some sense irrelevant as long as you are consistent in how you handle them (and, in particular, you take the limit of removing the UV cutoff in a controlled way). It's this last part -- the idea that the UV cutoff doesn't fundamentally affect the predictions as long as you take it to infinity in the right way -- that I think is the key tenet of the Wilsonian picture, and the one that makes it so appealing.
It's also worth noting that, in a certain sense, the Wilsonian approach *is* what effective field theory is about. You don't know the UV, you don't care about the UV, and you're going to write down an EFT that describes the physics as a effective description of the low-energy degrees of freedom. You match coefficients in the EFT by making sure that you can reproduce the known high-precision results from the UV (if you have them), and you make predictions for when you don't have access to the UV data. The Wilsonian RG is just a concrete, systematic way to do this when the UV is some sort of lattice or other regularised theory.
I think these points are worth emphasizing because I often find that discussions of the RG -- especially in the context of critical phenomena, which is where the Wilsonian ideas are perhaps most popular -- tend to get mired in the details of perturbation theory and the renormalisation group as a mathematical algorithm for modifying couplings. This can make the discussion abstract, and it can be easy to forget that the core idea -- that the physics at low energies is only dependent on the low-energy behaviour of the UV, and that the details of the cutoff don't matter as long as you are careful about how you remove them -- is, at its heart, a very simple and intuitive idea. It's a very powerful idea, and I think it's one that deserves to be more central in how we teach and discuss the foundations of QFT and the RG.

By integrating out the UV degrees of freedom in a systematic way, the resulting low-energy theory's critical exponents and other universal properties emerge naturally from the coarse-graining procedure, independent of the specific UV details (as long as the RG flow is well-defined).
